<reason>Both sides ran disciplined, well-shaped cases: A on accountability gaps, brittle judgment, escalation speed and norm-building; B on verification impossibility, the undefinability of "meaningful human control," command responsibility as sufficient, and the compliant-disarm-first asymmetry. B's best work was the Ottawa/cluster-munitions comeback, which converted A's flip into evidence for its own verification thesis, and the closing's genuinely real distinction between verifying a presence and proving a negative. But A controlled the decisive clash. A's landmine flip forced B onto the back foot; A's Pressure Questions were precisely targeted at B's two burdens (name a defendant, name a restraint that survives your own objection), and B's honest answer to Q2 — mandatory human review of context before any engagement against personnel — handed A the collapse move: B's own proposal is a restatement of meaningful human control, meaning B ends up arguing about enforcement architecture rather than defending the weapon class the motion targets. A also landed the log-integrity turn (audit logs are written by the software being audited), which B's closing acknowledges but never resolves for its own regime. B's residual point — that A never drafted the Phalanx exception — is partly answered by A's "human targets in open environments" line plus the chemical-weapons drafting analogy. A paid a real execution cost for two clipped turns, which cost it the crisp asymmetry weighing twice, and that keeps this from being a solid win; but on the motion as written, A gave the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's closing exploitation of B's Rebuttal 2 answer: B, pressed to name a restraint surviving its own verification objection, proposed mandatory human review of context before engagement against personnel — which A showed is the motion itself, reducing B's remaining case to packaging. B's presence-versus-absence enforcement reply was sharp but did not restore a live defence of the weapon class.</best_rebuttal>
